1.explanation: The heart of the bug lies in the TypeScript language definition (the default-exported function in src/languages/typescript.js). That module builds on the JavaScript grammar but never adds a mode to recognize full generic identifiers (it simply reuses JS keyword/identifier rules). As a result, when the generic name contains a lowercase-to-uppercase boundary (e.g. “OutT”), the built-in IDENT_RE from ecmascript.js (`[A-Za-z$_][0-9A-Za-z$_]*`) is never applied in the generics context, and the highlighter splits the token at the uppercase boundary. To fix, we must augment the TS grammar in the default export so that generic type parameters are lexed by IDENT_RE as a single token (for example by injecting a `<IDENT_RE(?:\s*,\s*IDENT_RE)*>` mode into tsLanguage.contains), ensuring full camel-case names like OutT are highlighted consistently.

2.explanation: The core of the TypeScript grammar (the default-exported function in src/languages/typescript.js) composes and tweaks the JavaScript grammar to support TypeScript constructs, including generic parameters. Because the highlighting issue manifests in how generic identifiers (like “OutT”) are tokenized and colored, the fault lies in the language definition’s modes for generics—which are initialized in the default export—and potentially the underlying IDENT_RE from ecmascript.js. Fixing the camel-case split will require adjusting the generic-parameter handling inside the default function (or the imported JavaScript grammar), so that multi-part identifiers like “OutT” are recognized as a single unit rather than two separate tokens.
2.bug_scenario: When highlighting TypeScript generic type parameters in code like “type ParseFunc<OutT, InT> = …”, only the first camel-case component (“Out”) is picked up by the highlighter and colored as a type, while the trailing uppercase letter (“T”) is left unstyled. The user expects the entire identifier “OutT” or “InT” to be treated as a single token and highlighted uniformly.
